newsitem.title: USA: Czech crown on path to equilibrium - U.S. analysts.
newsitem.headline: Czech crown on path to equilibrium - U.S. analysts.

text.p: The Czech crown, which tumbled after the Czech National Bank (CNB) let it float freely on Monday, should stabilize at a sustainable, or equilibrium, level, U.S. analysts said Tuesday.

Alberto Ades, emerging markets currency economist at Goldman, Sachs and Co Inc, said he was not concerned about the crown drop to around 19.5 crowns per mark on Tuesday, more that 11 percent below its former basket.
"The trading puts it fairly close to what we see as the long-run equilibrium for the currency," Ades said.
Late Monday, the central bank eliminated the band within which the crown traded against a mark/dollar basket, and said the currency would now be cited relative to the mark.

Goldman, Sachs estimated in March the crown to be 18 percent overvalued, with long-run equilibrium value of 116 against a basket of currencies, but the firm had not yet recalculated an equilibrium value against the mark, Ades said.
"It's on its way to equilibrium," Ades said, adding that the movements may not have ended. "We don't have an official forecast, but we would anticipate the currency to get closer to fair value."

Luis R. Luis, head of emerging market analysis at Scudder Stevens & Clark, said that while foreign investors had been cautious about holding Czech equity and debt assets, many will regard prices as being attractive.
He said that many currencies tend to overshoot after a sharp move, and that investors would be watching for that pattern, but that the crown would likely find stability.
"To the extent that the (CNB) let rates relatively free in the secondary markets, we should see the currency stabilize after some overshooting," Luis said.
Luis said the Czech central bank was likely to tread lightly in currency markets, and use interest rates to help support the crown.
"My sense is that the central bank will not do any sizable (direct) intervention," Luis said. "They will use monetary policy, and do some measured intervention, timing it for maximum impact."
Richard Segal, head of fixed income research at Santander Investment, said the crown might decline slightly further, but added that current levels seemed appropriate.
"This should help to address what's happening in the Czech republic," Segal said.
